activity_context.topic_title: Changing a Basis Using the Change-of-Coordinates Matrix

examples.knowledge_point: Finding the Coordinates of a Vector in a New Basis Given Its Coordinates in Another Basis
examples.problem:
The bases $\mathcal{B}$ and $\mathcal{C}$ of $\mathbb{R}^2$ and the coordinates of the vector $\mathbf{x}$ relative to the basis $\mathcal{B}$ are given below. Find $[\mathbf{x}]_{\mathcal{C}}.$ 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14066197/assets/c6c10ed068cfde656d178c98eb4af979563efc82d589f750b8fa92973f362e2a.png)
examples.worked_solution:
Let's denote the vectors of $\mathcal{B}$ and $\mathcal{C}$ as $\{ \mathbf{b}_1,\mathbf{b}_2 \}$ and $\{ \mathbf{c}_1,\mathbf{c}_2 \},$ respectively.

The change-of-coordinates matrix from $\mathcal{B}$ to $\mathcal{C}$ is a matrix whose columns are the vectors of $\mathcal{B}$ relative to the basis $\mathcal{C}.$

So, we need to find the coordinates of $\mathbf{b}_1$ and $\mathbf{b}_2$ relative to the basis $\mathcal{C}.$ We can do this simultaneously by considering the matrix
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14066197/assets/034a2a4079120d719f9061c339899f9aed9b50a765200291ca15c500ef647a70.png)

Reducing the left-hand side to reduced row-echelon form using Gaussian elimination, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 1 & 1 \\ 6 & 13 & 1 & -1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-6){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & -5 & -7\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}+(-2){R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 11 & 15 \\ 0 & 1 & -5 & -7\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the change-of-coordinates matrix $P_{\small\mathcal{B}\to\mathcal{C}}$ is
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14066197/assets/8d07812ea170bcbb56264468f4cfd0fa8b88cf4f68f9b50d35f61e9e33de45c3.png)

Finally, we compute $[\,\mathbf{x}\,]_{\mathcal{C}}\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}[\,x\,]_{C} & ={P}_{B\to C}[\,x\,]_{B} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}11 & 15 \\ -5 & -7\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-7 \\ 3\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

feedback.problem:
$$
B={[\begin{aligned}5 \\ -3\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}-7 \\ 6\end{aligned}]},\,[x]_{S}=[\begin{aligned}18 \\ -9\end{aligned}]
$$

The basis $B$ of ${R}^{2}$ and the coordinates of the vector $x$ relative to the standard basis $S$ are given above. Find $[x]_{B}.$
feedback.worked_solution:
We will use the change-of-coordinates formula in the form

$$
[\,x\,]_{B}={P}_{S\to B}[\,x\,]_{S}.
$$

First, recall that the change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $S$ is the matrix whose columns are the vectors of $B$ relative to the standard basis $S.$ As a result, we have

$$
{P}_{B\to S}=[\begin{aligned}5 & -7 \\ -3 & 6\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, we need to find the change-of-coordinates matrix ${P}_{S\to B}$ from $S$ to $B.$ To do that, we compute the inverse of ${P}_{B\to S}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{S\to B} & ={P}_{B\to S}^{-1} \\  & ={[\begin{aligned}5 & -7 \\ -3 & 6\end{aligned}]}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{5\cdot 6-(-7)\cdot (-3)}[\begin{aligned}6 & 7 \\ 3 & 5\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{3} & \frac{7}{9} \\ \frac{1}{3} & \frac{5}{9}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we compute $[\,x\,]_{B}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}[\,x\,]_{B} & ={P}_{S\to B}[\,x\,]_{S} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{3} & \frac{7}{9} \\ \frac{1}{3} & \frac{5}{9}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}18 \\ -9\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$
